Senses.Explanation: Literally, to lift (提) and hold (持). The expression occurs 1,140 times in 261 allowlisted texts, with some false substring matches across word boundaries such as a name ending in the graph for 'raise' (提) followed by the graph for 'carry' (持). In its recurrent Chan use, a master holds up and maintains 'this matter,' the ancestral seal, or the essentials of the school before others. A teaching-seat record says the master came two thousand leagues to reside at a monastery solely to maintain this matter, then raised the whisk and said, 'Look! Look!' Other records use the verb when commenting on Mazu's sickbed answer and on how the ancients presented the cases. Thus the corpus bends an ordinary support verb into a public description of maintaining and presenting the lineage's recorded matter.
Senses.Note: No second sense is warranted: different objects and approving or critical appraisals are different deployments of the same act. Literal boundary collisions such as 'Bodhi carried a bowl' (菩提持鉢) were excluded from evidence and counts used for semantic conclusions.

Occurrences.Kwic: 二千里遠來住山，單單地提持此事。舉拂子曰：看！看！印文已露。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A residence-at-the-monastery statement directly joins maintaining this matter to raising the whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 荷負宗乘提持祖印。有時放行。同彼同此。見隨類身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse pairs bearing the school with maintaining the ancestral seal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人得意之後不忘利生。直入深山提持宗要。山僧暗昧。豈敢仰攀。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse applies the verb to maintaining the essentials of the school in a mountain residence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云：「馬師病裏竭力提持，全身為人，叵耐不遇知音。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master explicitly appraises Mazu's sickbed answer as strenuous holding-up.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖師千七百則葛藤，是祭鬼神底器具，用之則禍生。古人恁麼提持，也覺大有徑庭，不近人情。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A critical comment applies the same verb to how the ancients presented the seventeen hundred cases.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to bring up and call attention to
Senses.Explanation: The compound is a transitive verb for bringing something up and calling attention to it, whether a teacher prompts another person or a person repeatedly brings up a saying or matter. The clearest in-record explanation occurs when a monk asks the teacher to prompt him concerning the lineage matter; the teacher calls him nearer and says, “this is prompting you” (這個是提撕汝). Hongzhi describes two participants each putting out a hand and bringing up this matter (各出一隻手，提撕此事). Dahui reports the act of going once through an old teacher's saying (以古人言句提撕一遍), elsewhere says simply to bring it up from time to time (但自時時提撕), and enumerates walking, sitting, joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, and responsive dealings as occasions for bringing it up. Wumen distinguishes those who pick up Zhaozhou's answer from those who bring it under examination, saying that many do each. The term occurs 521 times in 191 allowlisted files and ranges across requests for prompting, memorial thanks for a teacher's repeated prompting, comments on cases, and instructions to bring up a word or saying.
Senses.Note: The entry translates the verb in each grammatical setting. It does not turn repeated attention to a word or saying into a named regimen or imported category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問宗乘中事乞和尚提撕師云是什麼師却喚近前這個是提撕汝喚作宗乘中事即不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under the section “Admonitions on Asking Questions,” a monk asks for prompting about the lineage matter. The teacher asks what it is, calls him closer, and says, “this is prompting you; you may not call it the lineage matter.” This direct explanation is retained without assigning an uncertain roster identity.

Occurrences.Kwic: 可謂。一抑一揚。一奪一縱。各出一隻手。提撕此事。且道。是什麼事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi comments on a recorded exchange: “It may be called one pressing down and one raising up, one taking and one releasing; each puts out one hand and brings up this matter. Say, what matter is it?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉時須要以眼顧視。只是以古人言句提撕一遍。喚作不在言句上。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui critically reports a contemporary deployment: at the time of raising a case, people look with their eyes, go once through an old teacher's saying, and call that “not resting on words.” The occurrence documents the verb; the entry does not endorse the reported claim.

Occurrences.Kwic: 也不著忘懷。也不著著意。但自時時提撕。妄念起時。亦不得將心止遏。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's literal instruction: “Do not set yourself on forgetting it and do not set yourself on forcing attention; just bring it up from time to time. When wandering thoughts arise, do not use mind to suppress them.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 只如僧問趙州：狗子還有佛性也無？州云：無。諸方拈者甚多，提撕者不少。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen cites the public case: a monk asks Zhaozhou, “Does a dog have buddha-nature or not?” Zhaozhou says, “no.” Wumen adds, “many throughout the regions pick it up; not a few bring it under examination.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 先師老和尚某奉侍日久多蒙苦口提撕追遠之誠何可忘也
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Record of Chan Master Foyan of Longmen, the speaker recalls long service to his former teacher and says he often received the teacher's painstaking verbal prompting. The line is a memorial statement, so the former teacher is not assigned as its speaker.

Senses.Explanation: To raise, lift up, or bring something forward. The expression occurs 1,685 times in 307 allowlisted texts. In public encounters the object is often concrete and made visible: a whisk becomes the object of a question, a newcomer raises a sitting cloth and makes a circle, Nanquan raises the disputed cat and asks the assembly to speak, Yinfeng raises his rosary when asked his age, and a Chan visitor raises a tea cup when asked about “the other side.” Later instructional records use the same raising action with a saying or question as object: Mingben tells an assembly to bring forward a saying without flavor, the investigated saying, or the full question “the myriad things return to one; where does the one return?” Physical and discursive objects do not create different lexical actions. The Chan deviation is the density with which raising an object or matter becomes a visible or verbal move inside public exchange and instruction.
Senses.Note: The former concrete/abstract split was a literal-versus-extended reading of the same raising action and is merged. Compare whisk (拂子), sitting cloth (坐具), upright raising (豎起), raised saying (話頭), investigated saying (所參話), and lifting or citing (舉起). No fixed spiritual force is assigned to raising either kind of object.

Occurrences.Kwic: 光拈得拂子。趂至僧堂前。見師乃提起拂子曰。闍黎喚這箇作甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The whisk is physically lifted and immediately made the object of a question.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一日，六人新到相看，五人作禮，一人提起坐具，作一圓相。師云：我聞有一隻獵狗甚惡。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A newcomer lifts the sitting cloth and makes a circle during an encounter with Huangbo.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師因兩堂爭猫兒，師遂提起猫兒云：大眾！道得即不斬，道不得即斬。眾無語，師遂斬之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Nanquan physically lifts the cat and addresses the assembly in the public case.

Occurrences.Kwic: 韓文公一日相訪。問師。春秋多少。師提起數珠。曰。會麼。公曰。不會。師曰。晝夜一百八。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yinfeng lifts a rosary as his response to a question about his age.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單單提起箇無義味話頭，自最初一日立定脚頭，不得分毫移動，密密與之做向前去，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mingben's address commands bringing forward a saying without flavor. The object is discursive rather than physical, but the raising verb remains the same.

Occurrences.Kwic: 休息萬慮，單單提起箇所參話，向三根椽下盡其形命，一生了辨，不為分外。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A separate address names the object as the saying being investigated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 十二時中單單提起箇萬法歸一、一歸何處話，行疑坐疑，猛利無間，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text supplies the complete question that is to be brought forward.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪客提起茶甌。泉曰：「此猶是這邊事，那邊事作麼生？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A Chan visitor raises a tea cup in response to Nanquan's question; Nanquan says this is still the affair on this side and asks about the other side.
